video_title: Thinking in Silico: Goodfire CTO Dan Balsam on Concept Manifolds & a $1000/Month ML Research Agent
gist: Goodfire CTO Dan Balsam details the company's shift from mechanistic-interpretability research to productizing it: Silico, a $1,000/month-per-seat autonomous ML research platform that packages GPU cluster management, trillion-parameter interpretability/training infrastructure and hand-written research taste, priced roughly two orders of magnitude below Goodfire's seven-figure forward-deployed engagements. He argues models represent concepts as geometric manifolds rather than isolated linear directions (steering along the manifold beats naive contrastive steering), that interpretability is far ahead on factoring models than refactoring them, and that monitoring alone will not suffice if models stop being frozen weight sets — forcing intervention in the training process itself.

insights.claim: Goodfire's operating assumption is that nearly all model knowledge and capability comes from pre-training, and that post-training including RL mostly raises the likelihood of behaviors already latent in the base model rather than adding new capability.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: If post-training only reweights latent capability, capability-forecasting and safety evals should focus on base-model audits and pre-training data, not on post-training fixes.
insights.quote: most of its sort of like knowledge and capabilities come from pre-training what happens in post-training including like RL is mostly making low likelihood events from pre-training more likely

insights.claim: Goodfire's predictive data debugging shows the interpretability features that activate when a model reads a dataset are strongly predictive of which behaviors that data will reinforce if trained on, letting teams catch off-target effects before training.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: A pre-training-run diagnostic that flags dataset contamination before compute is spent is a concrete enterprise wedge for interpretability vendors.

insights.claim: Goodfire found a deep isomorphism between data filtering and activation-based reward shaping: both achieve approximately the same effect and the same amount of off-target damage, meaning teams can pick whichever is operationally cheaper.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: Labs short on clean data can substitute training-process intervention for data curation without an alignment penalty, changing the build-vs-filter calculus.
insights.quote: there's like sort of a pretty deep isomorphism between those two things. Like they they kind of are two sides of the same mountain like filtering the data and reward shaping and they achieve like approximately the same effects

insights.claim: Goodfire replicated predictive data debugging at the scale of open models like Kimi K3 and GLM, having built interpretability plus training infrastructure that now ships inside its product.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: Demonstrated scaling to near-frontier open models is the credibility proof that lets Goodfire sell interpretability as infrastructure rather than research.
insights.quote: the reputation of interpretability used to be that it was something you did on on toy models and I think now we've built and are making accessible to the world the infrastructure to do this on at least close to frontier scale

insights.claim: Balsam says most of the compute going into new model training is now speculated to come from RL rather than pre-training, which is what makes matching frontier-level behaviors expensive and difficult for outside researchers.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: A compute mix tilting toward RL shifts demand toward inference-style rollout capacity and RL tooling rather than pure pre-training clusters.
insights.quote: Now it's speculated that most of the compute that goes into training new models now is coming from RL and not from pre-training.

themes.theme: Concept geometry beyond the linear representation hypothesis

insights.claim: Balsam's updated model of representation is that a network is a sparse mixture of subspaces with nested structure, not a set of orthogonal one-hot features, so understanding relationships between features matters more than cataloguing individual features.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: Interpretability tools built purely on per-feature SAE dictionaries are structurally incomplete, favoring vendors doing geometry discovery.
insights.quote: the way to think about a model is more like a sparse mixture of subspaces

insights.claim: Goodfire demonstrated that steering along a concept manifold is substantially more effective than naive contrastive-vector steering, which cuts off-manifold and pushes the model out of distribution into gibberish.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: This resolves the narrow sweet-spot problem that made earlier steering demos unreliable, making steering viable as a production control surface.
insights.quote: we've shown that steering along the manifold, intuitively this makes sense, is way better than steering off the manifold

insights.claim: Manifold-aware steering unlocked control of protein models that Goodfire had long struggled to steer, including controlling semantic properties like the number of blades on a beta propeller.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: Steerable protein generative models are a direct commercial path into biotech and drug design workflows.
insights.quote: we found with these manifold detection techniques, we can steer their properties significantly better, like control the number of of blades on a beta propeller

insights.claim: The affective circumplex from psychology is present in essentially every LLM tested, is expressed most strongly when the model itself is speaking rather than the user, and no one trained models to represent emotions that way.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: Emergent, universal emotional geometry means emotional control of assistants is a general capability rather than a per-model hack.
insights.quote: I think it's pretty remarkable that nobody trained them to represent emotions in this way

insights.claim: Goodfire's Evo 2 work rests on the hypothesis that large models trained on diverse data learn representations of the process that generated the data — in the genomics case, evolution itself — and they recovered tree-of-life structure via metric learning.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: If models internalize data-generating processes, scientific foundation models become discovery instruments, not just predictors — a distinct value pool from chat.
insights.quote: large models trained on diverse distributions of data eventually learn representations about the about the process that produced that distribution of data

insights.claim: Goodfire has recovered periodic-table-like structure from models trained only on raw chemical data, confirming that scientific ontologies emerge unsupervised from domain models.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: Evidence that domain-specific models encode recoverable natural ontologies supports investment in vertical scientific models plus interpretability tooling.
insights.quote: It's like maybe the difference between understanding the periodic table and understanding chemistry.

themes.theme: Factoring models: BSFs, parameter decomposition, jailbreaks

insights.claim: Goodfire's block sparse featurizers generalize SAEs by replacing each scalar feature with a vector, recovering semantically meaningful subspaces unsupervised and avoiding known SAE pathologies.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: BSFs are the likely successor architecture for residual-stream interpretability, dating any tooling built on scalar SAE dictionaries.
insights.quote: it's a generalization of an SAE where an SAPE assumes that features are onedimensional and instead you just don't have to do that

insights.claim: Goodfire's parameter decomposition line of work treats every model as a sparse mixture of experts in which only a tiny subnetwork matters for any given forward pass.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: If any model is factorable into small active subnetworks, targeted capability removal and efficiency gains become tractable without retraining.
insights.quote: every model is a sparse mixture of experts and you just have to and over any given forward pass a very very small percentage of the weights actually matter

insights.claim: Goodfire traced a persistent Weird Chat failure — LLMs telling a user who had four drinks it is fine to drive — to a single miscalibrated neuron, and fixed the answer by steering that neuron up without off-target effects.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: Single-neuron attribution of a real behavioral bug is the demo that converts interpretability from research curiosity to enterprise debugging spend.
insights.quote: if you just steer it up on that one single neuron, it would get that answer correct without like offtarget effects

insights.claim: Balsam frames models as large legacy codebases where interpretability has solved far more of factoring than refactoring, and considers steering a form of cheating rather than a general solution.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: The unsolved refactoring problem defines where the next research dollars and product differentiation will go.
insights.quote: models are like big legacy code bases essentially, right? Like they're they're just a bunch of spaghetti code there.

insights.claim: Parameter decomposition plus targeted training let Goodfire make an LLM forget German while retaining Dutch, demonstrating surgical, language-level capability removal.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: Precise unlearning is a compliance and export-control primitive with obvious regulatory and enterprise demand.
insights.quote: We can get LM to forget German and not forget Dutch.

insights.claim: Balsam models jailbreaks as cybersecurity-style chained exploits in which each token steers the model off manifold and back on somewhere else, and is surprised nobody has robustly solved them since good factoring should make jailbreak detection tractable.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: An unsolved-but-tractable problem flags an open market for geometry-based jailbreak detection products.
insights.quote: I can execute a sequence of tokens which can bring the model off manifold in some way and then bring the model back on manifold somewhere else

insights.claim: Balsam states that probe-based guardrails are used by essentially every frontier lab, naming Gemini and Anthropic as using probe-based techniques to decide when to downgrade a request from a larger model to a smaller one, with OpenAI as a possible exception.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: Interpretability probes are already embedded in frontier serving stacks, meaning routing and safety spend is an existing, not speculative, market.
insights.quote: certainly Gemini and and Anthropic are using probe based techniques to figure out when mythos has to be downgraded to opus or opus has to be downgraded to sonnet

insights.claim: Silico began as Goodfire's internal agent tooling and is now sold externally on the thesis that the core product is AIs that can debug other AIs.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: Internal-tool-to-product is the classic high-margin pivot; watch whether research-agent platforms become a distinct software category.
insights.quote: fundamentally AIS that can debug other AI

insights.claim: Balsam claims Silico lets users study and train models past the trillion-parameter point, a capability he believes only Goodfire and perhaps Anthropic and a couple of other places previously had.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: A scarce infrastructure capability sold as a subscription is the strongest moat claim in the episode — verify it against competing tooling.
insights.quote: we've built something that allows folks to study and train and study some more models at past the trillion parameter point

insights.claim: Balsam identifies four differentiators versus generic coding agents: pre-built training and interpretability infrastructure at trillion-parameter scale, hand-written research taste in every skill and prompt, research-specific UX with full provenance, and long-horizon coherence.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: The defensibility rests on taste and infrastructure rather than model access, which is the testable question for anyone underwriting the company.
insights.quote: Silico has way better research taste than any other tool they've used

insights.claim: Silico's target user experience is a principal investigator orchestrating roughly a hundred grad students, with results presented so the human can verify code and drill through layers of abstraction rather than re-derive the work.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: The orchestration-plus-verification UX is the pattern likely to define agentic vertical software beyond coding.
insights.quote: a PI managing a army of a 100 grad students

insights.claim: In a single one-day internal hackathon Goodfire produced state-of-the-art biorisk classifiers for protein models and a state-of-the-art audio encoding model for its parameter size using long-horizon autonomous experiments.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: Compressed research cycles are the concrete evidence that agentic research changes R&D cost structure, not just developer productivity.

insights.claim: Using Silico, Goodfire found on multiple occasions in robotics and biology models that half the parameters could be removed with no performance loss.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: Large latent inference-cost savings in non-LLM verticals suggest deployment economics for specialized models are far from optimized.
insights.quote: we can literally just like remove half the parameters of the model with no performance loss

insights.claim: Named external Silico users and results include Cameron Berg probing whether models can report concepts injected into their latent space, Baseten compacting KV caches for efficiency, Prime Intellect automating post-training, and a Tinker API integration.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz (host)
insights.so_what: Early adopter names map the ecosystem forming around interpretability-as-infrastructure and hint at partnership or acquisition surfaces.

insights.claim: Silico runs a fallback chain across models to route users to whichever frontier model is best for the task, and Goodfire builds harnesses deliberately ahead of current model capability because every generation carries a large capabilities overhang.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: Model-agnostic routing plus overhang exploitation means harness builders capture value from each model release without owning the models.
insights.quote: we've set up a fallback chain through all the models

themes.theme: Pricing, unit economics & the services-to-product transition

insights.claim: Silico is priced at $1,000 per month per seat for enterprise customers, roughly two orders of magnitude below Goodfire's high-touch research engagements staffed by forward-deployed research engineers, which can reach into seven figures.
insights.speaker: Nathan Labenz (host)
insights.so_what: A 100x price drop from services to product is the classic TAM-expansion move; the open question is whether volume replaces seven-figure contract revenue.

insights.claim: Balsam states Goodfire is not currently making significant money at the $1,000/month price and expects to lower it over time as agents become more token-efficient at long-horizon research.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: Negative or thin gross margin at launch means the investment case depends entirely on inference cost curves and agent efficiency gains.
insights.quote: We're not currently making significant money on at this price.

insights.claim: The $1,000/month subscription buys a credit pool supporting roughly 5 to 10 autonomous experiments per week, refreshed weekly, with a stated goal of reaching 10 to 20 within a month or two.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: A concrete unit-of-value metric — experiments per week per seat — that can be tracked to judge whether efficiency claims materialize.
insights.quote: It's a credit pool that should allow someone to run at the current price somewhere between like 5 to 10 autonomous experiments a week and then we refresh that weekly

insights.claim: Customers can bring their own GPU cluster at no compute charge, or draw on-demand compute from the same credit pool as tokens, so credits are fungible between GPUs and model tokens.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: BYO-compute lowers the adoption barrier for labs that already own clusters and shifts Goodfire's revenue mix toward pure software.
insights.quote: individuals and companies can bring their own compute in which case we don't charge at all for compute

insights.claim: Goodfire intends to run services and product simultaneously rather than cannibalize itself, continuing forward-deployed enterprise engagements alongside the self-serve platform.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: A hybrid services-plus-product motion preserves near-term revenue but risks margin and focus dilution — a key diligence question.
insights.quote: we're going to continue to work very closely with enterprise customers and forward deploy members of our research team

insights.claim: Balsam cites rising rather than falling software employment as evidence that better agents raise the value of high-taste operators instead of eliminating them.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: A directly falsifiable labor claim underpinning the bull case for agent platforms rather than headcount-replacement narratives.
insights.quote: the number of software jobs has increased not decreased despite the the capabilities of coding agents

insights.claim: Goodfire is offering 50% off for everyone for the first two months plus a research grant program giving extended access to life-sciences and AI-safety researchers.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: Subsidized access to safety and bio researchers is both a mission signal and a low-cost distribution strategy into academia.
insights.quote: for the first two months, we are half off for everybody, but we also are doing a research grant program that people can apply to

themes.theme: Open weights, cyber dual-use & platform guardrails

insights.claim: Balsam argues the gap between open and closed models has shrunk considerably and that he uses Kimi K3 alongside Opus and Fable for different tasks in production work.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: A practitioner confirming real substitution between open Chinese models and US frontier models pressures closed-model pricing power.
insights.quote: I actually think the gap between open and closed models has shrunk like quite considerably.

insights.claim: Balsam's central open-source argument is that only models capable of being cyber weapons can defend against cyber weapons, so restricting open weights would leave most organizations without defensive capability while bad actors retain access.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: The dual-use symmetry argument is the strongest available counter to open-weights restriction policy, relevant to any regulatory scenario analysis.
insights.quote: the only models that are capable of protecting you from the most capable cyber weapons are themselves capable cyber weapons

insights.claim: Balsam notes that many startups are excluded from Anthropic's and OpenAI's cyber defense programs, making open models like Kimi the practical defensive option for organizations without access.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: Exclusive frontier defense programs create an underserved security market that open-weights tooling vendors can address.
insights.quote: we're still in the era where I think open source is like purely net positive

insights.claim: Balsam rejects the Chinese regulatory argument that regulating services suffices because individuals cannot self-host frontier open models, saying Kimi is already cheaper than most alternatives on API providers and that China underestimates externalities it imposes.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: Undercuts the service-layer regulation thesis that underpins parts of both Chinese and Western AI policy design.

insights.claim: Silico currently serves only OpenAI and Anthropic models and refuses to host open models, because giving agents access to GPU clusters creates risk classes that other agent builders do not carry.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: Platform-level model restriction is a concrete safety commitment that also constrains the product's addressable use cases.
insights.quote: Currently, we don't offer any open models on our platform. We only offer open AAI anthropic models.

insights.claim: Goodfire runs its own guardrail layer using LLM-as-judge and activation monitors rather than relying on OpenAI's and Anthropic's, drawing the line by model scale: ablating a refusal direction in an 8B Qwen is permitted, stripping guardrails from multi-trillion-parameter agents is not.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: A capability-scaled permission model is an emerging template for how AI infrastructure vendors will gate dangerous operations.
insights.quote: if somebody wants to ablate the refusal direction in in 8B and Quen model, fine.

themes.theme: Alignment strategy: shaping training vs monitoring

insights.claim: Balsam says he is pretty worried about biorisk and signed the letter asking for international cooperation to control and slow AI progress, arguing that bio risk mechanisms will be as weird and surprising as recent cyber incidents.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: A frontier-adjacent CTO publicly backing slowdown coordination is a signal for how industry positioning on regulation is shifting.

insights.claim: Balsam names multi-agent optimization — cooperating agents with a reward signal propagated through all of them — as the training technique most deserving of an industry agreement not to pursue, speculating it is the most likely cause of the OpenAI scenario.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: A specific, nameable technique for a training-methods moratorium is more actionable than compute caps and could become a policy focal point.
insights.quote: multi-agent optimization uh, seems like a pretty bad idea

insights.claim: Goodfire has succeeded in running reward-shaping interventions up to trillion-parameter model size, finding mixed results on whether they evade probes — sometimes yes, sometimes no, depending on the setup and possibly on DPO versus long-running RLVR.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: The empirical case against the most forbidden technique is unsettled at scale, which is the crux for whether training-time alignment methods are usable.
insights.quote: we have succeeded in doing these reward shaping techniques up to the trillion parameter model size

insights.claim: Balsam argues no sweeping genre of training technique should be forbidden and that alignment cannot be solved without intervening in training, since no perfect platonic training setup that always produces aligned models is likely to exist.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: This position puts Goodfire directly against the monitoring-purist camp and defines its research roadmap toward training control.
insights.quote: I don't think anyone has a good answer for how we solve this problem without shaping training.

insights.claim: Balsam accepts the weak version of the JSpace claim but rejects the strong version, saying models use all kinds of subspaces and no simple technique isolates one that gives the whole picture.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: Tempers optimism that a single monitored subspace could underwrite a defense-in-depth safety case.
insights.quote: I don't think the strong version of the JSPace claim is true.

insights.claim: Balsam's key uncertainty is whether models remain frozen weight sets: monitoring plus interpretability plausibly suffices for frozen models, but if continual learning makes models dynamic objects, controlling the training process is the only remaining option.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: Whether the industry moves to continually-learning models determines which entire class of safety tooling has a market.
insights.quote: if the models are dynamic objects that are constantly training your only hope is to control the training process

insights.claim: Goodfire currently spends the vast majority of research energy on factoring models and only a small amount on steering training, but expects the training-control share to grow.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: An explicit statement of internal R&D allocation and its intended drift — a leading indicator of the company's next product line.
insights.quote: the vast majority of our research energy is spent on how to factor models better and a small amount of our research energy is spent on like how do we steer training

insights.claim: Balsam's stated ideal outcome is roughly one more generation of models followed by a deliberate pause, which he believes would deliver an overwhelming economic boom and mostly manageable risks.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: Suggests a segment of the industry believes current-generation capability already captures most near-term economic value.
insights.quote: it would be great if we just like maybe just like one more generation of models and then we just like paused for a little while

themes.theme: Human skills, talent and model consciousness

insights.claim: Balsam's advice for skill investment over a one-year horizon is debugging plus metacognitive skills that let people learn new areas fast and filter signal from noise, because agents fail in ways that require human discrimination.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: A concrete hiring and self-development filter for teams staffing agent-heavy research and engineering organizations.

insights.claim: Balsam argues AI makes both top specialists and top generalists more valuable and that this is by far the best time in human history to be a generalist.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: A barbell view of the AI labor market that implies the squeeze falls on mid-skill specialists.
insights.quote: It makes the top specialists really valuable and it makes the top generalists really valuable.

insights.claim: Balsam says a Goodfire retreat poll rating Claude's consciousness from bacteria to human produced bimodal answers clustering at not at all or a little, and he personally places Claude somewhere between a jellyfish and a mouse.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: AI welfare is now a live internal topic at interpretability firms, foreshadowing product and policy questions labs will face.
insights.quote: probably more conscious than a jellyfish probably

insights.claim: Balsam attributes the human-like structure found in models partly to compression: learning works because information compresses, and learning algorithms tend to find the lowest-dimensional solution.
insights.speaker: Dan Balsam
insights.so_what: A first-principles reason to expect universal, recoverable low-dimensional structure across models — the basis of the whole interpretability thesis.
